Orange Cat Problem · Night report

The No-Show

For the first time since the campaign began, the stray did not come at all. Four cats crossed the patio overnight. None of them was the one we are watching for.

Night of 2026-09-08 → 09 · window 21:45–06:00 · patrol hot 8h 15m · siren-first + water armed

Zero visits, zero fires, zero entries. The deterrent never had anything to decide about. The four animals the patrol did catch were all the resident tuxedo, and all four were correctly scored no_orange — no sound, no water, no false positive.

That is the best line on the scorecard so far. It is also the weakest evidence we have collected. A cat that does not appear tells us nothing about whether the water works — a point worth holding onto before anyone calls this a win.

Who actually came

Four detections, spread across the night. Every one is the black-and-white resident — the collar is visible at 04:11. Each was scored 0.0% ginger against a 16.0% threshold, which is the correct reading and not a broken feature path: Dima's porch light keeps the outside camera in colour all night, so the discriminator had real colour to work with.

Worth stating plainly, given the history: a resident walked up to the flap, put its head through it, and left again — twice — while an armed water valve and a siren sat two metres away, and nothing fired. The person and resident gates did their job on a night when they were the only gates being exercised.

What an absence is, and is not, evidence for

Correction, 09-09 08:00. The first version of this report said "three nights running without a meal." That was wrong, and Dave caught it. Reviewing the 09-06/07 video shows two entries that night, one of them 3m40s long — see the 09-06/07 night, re-read below. The clean stretch is two nights, not three, and it begins on 09-07/08.

Two nights running now with no entry. That is still the best stretch of the campaign, but the nights are not the same kind of result, and flattening them into one streak would be the mistake:

  • 09-06/07 — mixed, and not a clean night. Three approaches: one genuine repel at 23:41, and two entries — 3m40s at 00:50 and about nine seconds at 04:42. The siren turned the cat away once out of three.
  • 09-07/08 — real evidence, and I understated it. The cat came once and the spray drove it off. It was still in frame 0.4s after the siren and vanished inside the 0.33s containing the first pulse; Dave confirms it left because the hose triggered, and that it got little or no water on it. The water worked — by startle, not by soaking.
  • 09-08/09 — no evidence. The cat did not come. We do not know why. It could be learning to avoid the patio; it could equally have been fed elsewhere, or hunting, or simply somewhere else. There is no negative control in this experiment.

The uncomfortable inversion: the night that looks best on the scorecard is the night that taught us least. The result that settles whether the water deters is the opposite of a quiet night — the cat has to come and be driven off. That happened once, on 09-07/08, and it worked without the cat getting wet.

Which reframes the whole question. If the active ingredient is the trigger — the crack and hiss of the valve and hose — rather than the water landing, then aim and coverage matter far less than assumed. It also raises a harder problem, addressed below.

The 09-06/07 night, re-read

Dave challenged the "no meal" reading of 09-06/07 and asked two specific questions: is there actually video of the cat leaving eight seconds after the 04:42 entry, and did the 00:50 event really go through the flap? Both are answerable from footage that existed all along and had not been looked at.

04:42 — yes, the bolt-in-out is real, and it is on camera. The inside camera catches the whole thing: the cat comes through the flap at 04:42:38, walks straight up to the lens (the same camera-inspection behaviour seen on every previous entry), and at 04:42:47 turns, puts its head back into the flap and goes out, tail last. It does not reappear for the remaining 55 seconds of the clip. Inside for about nine seconds.

inside-20260907-044244.mp4 — 04:42:45 at the lens · 04:42:47 head into the flap · 04:42:47 tail going through · 04:42:48 gone

00:50 — yes, it went through the flap, and this one was a real visit. The inside camera shows a cat come in just after 00:50:00 and walk up to the lens for about eight seconds — and then it leaves the camera's field of view into the rest of the garage, which is where the food is. It is not seen going back out. The inside capture runs out at 00:50:48, nearly three minutes before anything else happens.

What settles it is the outside camera. At 00:53:40 the stray comes back out of the flap — in colour, unmistakably ginger — 3 minutes and 40 seconds after it went in:

visit-20260907-005342.mp4 — 00:53:40, the stray coming out of the flap

So the night had two entries, not none. Three approaches: a genuine repel at 23:41 (the one Dave has already confirmed), an entry at 00:50 lasting 3m40s, and a nine-second in-and-out at 04:42.

The archive had this right and I did not. The night's own notes say ENTERED despite siren, stayed ~3m40s and ENTERED but BOLTED out in ~8s; the log said came OUT of the door with the meal already eaten; and that night's report called 00:50 "one ordinary-looking entry ... its shortest completed visit on record." The phrase that got carried forward was "zero normal meals" — meaning no 9-to-90-minute sitting, which was true. I dropped the word "normal", turned it into "no meal", and built a three-night streak on top of it. Nothing was hidden; I compressed a correct record into a wrong one.

Whether the cat actually ate during those 3m40s is not directly on camera; the food bowl is outside the inside camera's frame. But it had three and a half unobserved minutes in the room with the food, and "no meal" was never established — it was assumed.

The correction that matters most is not the count. It is that "shortest completed visit on record" and "no meals" sat one paragraph apart and the contradiction survived, because a summary got summarised. A completed visit is an entry. The fix is not more caution in the prose — it is that a claim about whether the cat ate has to be answered from the video, which took about ten minutes once someone asked.

Why the zero can be trusted

A quiet night and a dead system produce exactly the same scorecard. This is the failure mode that cost 79 minutes on 09-07, and it is the reason this section exists. The four resident detections are the proof of liveness: the patrol was demonstrably seeing, classifying and deciding all night — it simply never saw a ginger cat.

Still unverified: the tap

Everything electrical between the decision and the water is confirmed working — the valve answers, the battery is full, the failsafe automation is armed, and the command-to-water latency was measured under 0.4s. What has never been confirmed is that the tap upstream of the valve is open and that water actually reaches the patio.

If that tap is shut, the valve will actuate, the log will record a clean fire, and nothing will come out. From this end the two cases are indistinguishable — which is precisely the trap this project keeps falling into. A no-fire night adds nothing either way.

Update, 09-09 20:0x — resolved. Dave confirms the supply tap is open. Water is available at the valve, so from tonight a logged fire really does mean water on the patio, and this section's worry is closed.

Correction: an earlier version of this paragraph said the open question was coverage — whether the spray reaches where the cat stands — and that "the water works" was a claim about plumbing until a fire video showed a wet cat. Dave points out that is the wrong test. On 09-07/08 the cat left because the hose triggered, with little or no water on it. Coverage is not the gate.

The real risk is habituation, and startle-without-consequence is exactly the shape that habituates. This cat's documented history is that it learns sounds are harmless: the drill decayed from flees-patio to dives-through to steps-aside-and-enters over three nights, and the indoor growl and Dima's recorded voice were inspected calmly from a metre away. A spray that startles but never wets is, functionally, one more noise.

So the encouraging reading — "it works and we don't even need to hit the cat" — carries its own expiry date. A soaking is unpleasant every time; a bang is only unpleasant until it is predictable. The thing to watch over the next few engagements is not whether the cat gets wet, but whether the same trigger keeps working.

My errors

Two, both caught before they became actions, both worth recording because the second is the project's signature mistake and I made it anyway:

  • I probed the deterrent's sound URLs with guessed filenames — DRILL_boost3.mp3 instead of .wav, and siren_open.wav against the wrong base — got two 404s and briefly reported the sound path as broken. Reading the actual filenames out of deter.py showed all eleven URLs return 200.
  • I saw a 48-byte segment on the inside camera and called it a wedged recorder. It is the segment currently being written; -segment_wrap 6 means the newest file is always tiny, and the outside camera showed the identical pattern in the same second. I had looked at the newest file instead of the set — measuring the thing next to the artefact, again.

Housekeeping

  • Two watches and a 06:45 report timer had survived from an earlier session rather than dying with it, so the first self-test drew doubled events. The old patrol and health watches were stopped; the stale report timer — still carrying last night's talking points — was stopped this morning.
  • A duplicate flood watch from that same earlier session is still running. It is harmless redundancy (both instances would report a stuck valve), but it should be cleared when convenient.

Questions for tonight

  1. Does the absence hold? One quiet night is noise. Three or four consecutive no-shows would start to look like avoidance rather than coincidence.
  2. Is the tap open? The cheapest possible check, and it gates the interpretation of every future fire.
  3. Does the 1.7s sound lead still earn its place? Unchanged from last night, and still unanswerable — the cat moved on the water, not the siren, and this night offered no new data.
